name: L10 · Generative AI & LLMs
description: GenAI families, how LLMs work, transformers, diffusion, using LLMs, pathology case study

cards.front: Where do generative AI and LLMs fit within AI?
cards.back:
Nested circles, from broadest to narrowest:

- **Artificial intelligence** – machines doing tasks that seem to need intelligence
- **Machine learning** – learns patterns from data instead of hand-written rules
- **Deep learning** – ML with large, many-layered neural networks
- **Generative AI** – creates **new content**: text, images, audio, code
- **Large language models (LLMs)** – generative models for **language**, trained on huge amounts of text

Everyday examples of GenAI: chat assistants (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini), writing help and autocomplete, translation, image generation, auto-captions and AI meeting notes.

cards.front: What is the difference between discriminative and generative AI?
cards.back:
| **Discriminative AI** | **Generative AI** |
|---|---|
| Learns to **tell categories apart** – answers "which one?" | Learns **what the data looks like** – and makes new data |
| Output: a **label**, e.g. "Malignant · 92 %" | Output: **new content**, e.g. a plain-language explanation of a biopsy report |

They use the **same deep-learning building blocks** with a different goal: **decide vs. create**.

cards.front: What kinds of output can generative AI produce?
cards.back:
- **Text** – chat, summaries, translation, emails (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini)
- **Images** – pictures from a text prompt (Stable Diffusion, DALL·E, Midjourney)
- **Code** – writing and fixing software (coding assistants)
- **Audio & speech** – natural voices, music, live transcription
- **Video** – short clips generated from text or an image
- **Science & medicine** – protein structures, drug candidates, synthetic medical images

cards.front: Give the short history of generative AI from 2014 to today.
cards.back:
- **2014 – GANs:** two networks compete (one fakes, one judges); the first realistic generated faces.
- **2017 – Transformer**, *"Attention Is All You Need"*: the architecture behind every LLM. **The turning point** – it made training on far more data practical.
- **2020 – GPT-3:** 175 billion parameters; fluent text from a short prompt.
- **2022 – Diffusion & ChatGPT:** image generation goes public; ChatGPT reaches millions of users in weeks.
- **2023 – Multimodal models:** GPT-4, Claude, Gemini, Llama read images as well as text.
- **2024–26 – Reasoning & agents:** models that work step by step and use tools to finish tasks.

cards.front: Name the five families of generative models and what each is good at.
cards.back:
| Family | Idea | Good at | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| **GANs** (2014) | A generator and a critic compete | Sharp images, image-to-image translation | StyleGAN, CycleGAN |
| **VAEs** (2013) | Compress to a short code, then rebuild | Smooth variations, spotting anomalies | Inside Stable Diffusion |
| **Diffusion** (2020) | Learn to remove noise step by step | Top-quality images and video | Stable Diffusion, DALL·E, Imagen |
| **Autoregressive transformers** (2018) | Predict the next token, repeat | Text, code, also audio | GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama |
| **Vision–language models** (2021) | Join images and text in one space | Image search, captions, chat about images | CLIP, CONCH, PathChat |

Real systems combine them: an image generator uses a **transformer** to read the prompt, a **VAE** to compress, and **diffusion** to paint.

cards.front: How does a GAN work? Use the forger and art-critic analogy.
cards.back:
- **Generator = the forger:** turns **random noise** into fake images.
- **Discriminator = the critic:** looks at real and fake images and outputs "real or fake?" (e.g. 0.3 = probably fake).
- **Feedback:** both learn every round – the critic gets better at spotting fakes, the forger gets better at fooling it.
- **Training ends** when the critic can no longer tell fake from real.

*In pathology:* generating synthetic tissue tiles for **rare subtypes**, and **stain normalisation** between labs (CycleGAN).

cards.front: How does an LLM generate text?
cards.back:
An LLM is a **next-word (next-token) predictor**.

*"The biopsy showed that the tumour was …"* → malignant 41 %, benign 27 %, invasive 14 %, small 9 %, other 9 %

Writing a whole answer:
1. **Score every possible next word** (a probability distribution).
2. **Pick one**, with a little randomness controlled by the **temperature** (low = safe and predictable, high = more creative and varied).
3. **Add it to the text and repeat.**

That's the whole trick – done with **billions of parameters**, trained on **trillions of words**.

cards.front: What are tokens and embeddings?
cards.back:
1. **Tokens:** text is split into **tokens** – a word or a piece of one ("Large language models read" → "Large", "language", "models", "read"; "tokens" → "tok" + "ens"). Each token gets an ID number.
2. **Embeddings:** each token is turned into a **vector** of thousands of numbers, e.g. "tumour" → [0.12, −0.83, 0.47, …] – its **meaning as coordinates**.
3. **Similar meanings sit close together** in this space: tumour, cancer, carcinoma form one group; cat, dog, horse another; Paris, Tokyo, Stockholm a third.

The **context window** is how many tokens the model can consider at once.

cards.front: What is attention, and why did the Transformer architecture matter?
cards.back:
**Attention:** every word looks at every other word and decides **which ones help explain it**.

*"The animal didn't cross the street because **it** was too tired"* → "it" attends most strongly to **animal**, medium to **tired**, weakly to **street** – so the model understands what "it" refers to.

**Transformer:**
- **Dozens of attention layers** stacked.
- Processes **all words at once** (in parallel, unlike an RNN going word by word) – so it **scales** to huge datasets.

**Not just words:** cut an image into **patches** and the same idea works – **Vision Transformers (ViT)**.

cards.front: What are the three stages of training an LLM assistant?
cards.back:
1. **Pre-training** – read a huge slice of the internet, books and code; learn to **predict the next token**. Result: a **base model** that knows language but isn't a helpful assistant yet.
2. **Instruction tuning** – train on many examples of good questions and answers written by people. Result: it **follows instructions** and answers like an assistant.
3. **Human feedback (RLHF)** – people **rank the model's answers**, and it learns to prefer the better ones. Result: more **helpful, honest and safe**.

Analogy: **read the library → apprenticeship → feedback from a mentor**.

cards.front: How do diffusion models generate images?
cards.back:
**Creating by removing noise:**

- **Training:** take millions of real images and **add noise step by step**; the model learns to **undo each step**.
- **Generating:** start from **pure noise** and remove it step by step (e.g. step 250 → 500 → 750 → final image), **guided by the text prompt** (e.g. "H&E-stained breast tissue, high magnification").

Examples: Stable Diffusion, DALL·E, Imagen – today's best for top-quality images and video.

cards.front: What are the four ways to put an LLM to work? Give an example of each.
cards.back:
From **easier and cheaper** to **more effort, more control**:

1. **Prompting** – clear instructions, context, examples and the format you want. *"You are a tutor. Explain this to a nurse in 5 bullet points."*
2. **RAG (retrieval-augmented generation)** – first **look up your own documents**, then answer from them. *A chatbot that answers from the hospital's own guidelines.* Reduces hallucination and keeps answers up to date.
3. **Fine-tuning** – train an existing model a little further on **your own examples**. *A model that writes in your clinic's report style.*
4. **Agents** – the LLM **plans steps and calls tools** (search, code, databases). *Pulls the data, runs the analysis, drafts the report.*

**Start simple** (prompting → RAG → fine-tuning → agents) and **always verify**.

cards.front: What can go wrong with generative AI?
cards.back:
- **Hallucinations** – confident but wrong answers; invented references.
- **Bias** – copies imbalances and stereotypes in its training data.
- **Privacy** – never paste patient or confidential data into public tools.
- **Copyright** – open questions about the training data and who owns the outputs.
- **Security** – jailbreaks and hidden **prompt-injection** instructions.
- **Cost & energy** – large models need a lot of computing power and electricity.

**Rule of thumb:** treat GenAI output as a **first draft** and keep a **human in the loop**.

cards.front: Why is reading a breast-cancer biopsy hard, and why is it a good target for AI?
cards.back:
A pathologist examines **H&E-stained tissue** and decides: benign or malignant? Which subtype? What grade?

Challenges:
- **Gigapixel images** – one scanned slide can hold **billions of pixels**; it is cut into thousands of tiles (e.g. 256 × 256 px).
- **Workload** – growing case numbers, too few pathologists.
- **Variability** – experts sometimes disagree on borderline cases.
- **Few labels** – expert annotations are slow and expensive.

cards.front: What are the five ways generative AI can help in pathology?
cards.back:
1. **Foundation models** – pre-trained on millions of **unlabelled** tissue images, reused for many tasks with few labels (*UNI, Virchow*).
2. **Image + text models** – classify or search images by **describing the classes in words**, zero-shot (*CONCH*).
3. **Chat assistants** – ask questions about an image in plain language and get explanations (*PathChat*).
4. **Synthetic data** – diffusion models or GANs create realistic tiles for **rare classes**, to augment small datasets and for teaching.
5. **Report drafting** – an LLM turns findings into a structured report or a patient-friendly summary; the **pathologist edits and signs**.

cards.front: Describe the foundation-model pipeline from slide to suggestion (e.g. UNI).
cards.back:
1. **Whole-slide image** – scan the glass slide.
2. **Tiles** – cut it into thousands of patches.
3. **Foundation model** (GenAI) – turns each tile into an **embedding**.
4. **Small classifier** – combines all tiles; **needs few labels**.
5. **Prediction + heatmap** – benign/malignant, subtype – and **where**.
6. **Draft report** (GenAI) – an LLM writes it; the **pathologist reviews**.

**Why it helps:** one pre-trained encoder serves many tasks (subtyping, grading, biomarkers) with far fewer labelled slides.
**UNI (Nature Medicine, 2024):** self-supervised on **100 million+ tissue images** from 100,000+ slides; outperformed earlier models across **34 tasks**.

cards.front: How can an image + text model like CONCH classify images without task-specific training?
cards.back:
**Images and text share one embedding space**, so you can classify by **finding the closest written description** (zero-shot):

- "an H&E image of invasive ductal carcinoma" → similarity **0.81** (best match)
- "an H&E image of benign breast tissue" → 0.12
- "an H&E image of invasive lobular carcinoma" → 0.07

→ predicted class: **invasive ductal carcinoma**. No new labelled training data is needed for new classes – you just write new descriptions.

**CONCH** (Nature Medicine, 2024) was trained on **1.17 million image–caption pairs**.

cards.front: What is PathChat?
cards.back:
A **chat assistant for pathology** (Nature, 2024): you ask about an image region in plain language, and it describes and interprets it, e.g. *"atypical epithelial cells infiltrate the stroma… features suggest invasive carcinoma – please confirm with a pathologist."*

- Built from a **pathology image encoder (UNI) + a large language model**.
- **Fine-tuned on 456,000+ image–instruction examples**.
- **Beat general assistants such as GPT-4V** on diagnostic questions in the study; pathologists preferred its answers.
- Uses: teaching, research, **human-in-the-loop** support.

cards.front: What must happen before pathology AI can reach patients?
cards.back:
The research is promising but **not yet autopilot**:

- **Validate** on other hospitals, scanners and stains (distribution shift).
- **Check for bias** across patient groups.
- **Explain decisions** – show *where* with heatmaps.
- **Regulatory approval** – FDA, EU MDR, EU AI Act.
- **AI suggests, the pathologist decides.**

(A 2025 benchmark of 19 models found the image + text model CONCH best overall on 31 tasks, with Virchow2 a close second.)

cards.front: What are the four things to remember about generative AI and LLMs?
cards.back:
1. **GenAI creates content.** An LLM is a **next-word predictor trained at enormous scale**.
2. **Transformers and attention** power both language and image models.
3. **Start simple:** prompting → RAG → fine-tuning → agents. **Always verify.**
4. In pathology, **foundation and image + text models cut the need for labels** – humans stay in charge.

cards.front: Define these LLM terms: token, context window, hallucination, RAG, multimodal, RLHF.
cards.back:
- **Token** – a piece of a word; the unit an LLM reads and writes.
- **Context window** – how much text (how many tokens) the model can consider at once.
- **Hallucination** – confident but false output.
- **RAG** – retrieval-augmented generation: retrieve trusted documents, then answer from them.
- **Multimodal** – works with text, images and audio.
- **RLHF** – reinforcement learning from human feedback: people rank answers and the model learns to prefer the better ones.

cards.front: What is the format of the written exam?
cards.back:
- **On campus, computer-based** (Inspera).
- **No coding.**
- Questions relate to the content of the course: **lectures, assignments and labs**.
- There can be **simple calculations** – bring your **own calculator** (mobile phones are **not** allowed as calculators).
- Register for the exam once the date is announced.

Past exams repeatedly ask about: the four views of AI and the Turing Test, environment properties and agent types, BFS/DFS/A* on a graph, first-order logic, genetic-algorithm calculations, supervised vs. unsupervised learning, and AI ethics.

cards.front: Course revision: give the key milestones of AI from 1950 to 2022.
cards.back:
- **1950** – Turing asks "Can machines think?" – the Turing Test
- **1956** – the Dartmouth workshop names the field "artificial intelligence"
- **1970s–80s** – the expert-systems boom, then funding cuts: the "AI winters"
- **1997** – IBM Deep Blue beats chess champion Kasparov
- **2012** – deep-learning breakthrough in image recognition (AlexNet)
- **2022** – ChatGPT brings generative AI to everyone

AI today is **narrow AI** – excellent at specific tasks (healthcare, finance, transport, recommendations, assistants); general human-level AI is still a goal. The course takes the **rational agent** view.
